doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Essential scales and chords to know
summary: Blue explains the chromatic, whole tone and diminished scales and the central role of the dominant seventh.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What is paramount stuff for you?

Well you’ve got to know, like for instance, all right like for instance when you have 2- 5’s, I don’t focus on the 2. It’s the 5’s that I’ll focus on. You know? Because the 2 is incorporated in the 5. You know? That’s one of the things. The — okay the most important scale that we have is the chromatic scale. Right? You know because each thing moves a half step down, a half step up, make all the difference. Okay? The next two important scales are the whole tone scale — it’s an even, it’s an even and equal scale, six tones in each one, everything is equal. And then the diminished, which comes from the whole tone. You know two from each — it’s minor thirds, so you have in each whole tone scale the two tones are a tri-tone apart. You know? And the dominant. Well you take a diminished chord and you lower any tone a half a step in a chromatic and you’ve got a dominant seventh. Now a dominant seventh is our most pivotal chord. All right? And what I mean by that is there are so many different combinations, you could play dominant, you could play minor, you could play diminished, you could play half-

diminished, you could play diminished whole tone. You know? Yeah. You put a flat nine or a sharp nine on there and you’ve got your diminished whole tone. You know so this is stuff you’ve got to know. Okay? And the most important thing is it’s all connected. Nothing is disjointed. It all comes from and leads to what is central. So yeah, so that’s some of the stuff that we want to know. Yeah. You want to know your basic, six basic jazz chords and your major, dominant, minor, half-diminished, diminished, and augmented. Then you’ll add other combinations you know, your triads, major triads, minor triads, major sixth and minor sixth, etc. You know, and how they all work. You know how they work. How do we do that? Well we isolate and we practice, but we listen. You’ve got to listen to the music. And we can learn how they’re used, how the language is used. You know to connect and have fun with it.
I’m glad you ended with that, to have fun with it.
I — yeah — I have fun with this stuff.
